User: I want to file my 2024 taxes correctly. I'm single in Austin TX. W-2 from Coastal Manufacturing: $68,200. Additional income: $16,300 (photography, 3 clients), $2,100 from Capital One 360, $420 from Merrill Edge. Home office: 120 sq ft exclusive; I pay $1,750/month for 740 sq ft. Deductions: $5,100 student loan interest (Nelnet, 2018–2021); $1,500 to Salvation Army have receipt; $1,050 unreimbursed expenses. Can you tell me what I can deduct, whether to itemize or take the standard deduction, how to tr

eat the home office, and what forms I need?
Assistant: Here’s how your 2024 federal return likely shakes out based on what you shared. I’ll note any places where a quick clarification could change the outcome.

What you can deduct (and how to treat each item)
- Student loan interest: You can deduct up to $2,500. Your income puts you in the 2024 phase‑out range for single filers (MAGI roughly $80,000–$95,000). With your numbers, you’ll likely get a partial deduction around $1,600–$2,200 (final amount depends

on your exact net business profit and half‑SE tax deduction).
- Charitable donations ($1,500 to Salvation Army): Deductible only if you itemize. You’ll almost certainly take the standard deduction (see below), so this likely won’t reduce your tax.
- “Unreimbursed expenses” ($1,050):
  - If these are W‑2 job expenses: not deductible in 2024 (suspended through 2025).
  - If these are photography business expenses: fully deductible on Schedule C.
- Home office (120 sq ft exclusive use in a 740 sq ft rental at

$1,750/mo):
  - Simplified method: $5/sq ft × 120 = $600 deduction.
  - Actual‑expense method: Allocate rent by square footage: 120/740 ≈ 16.2%. Annual rent $21,000 × 16.2% ≈ $3,405. This is much larger than the simplified method and is generally your better choice. You can also include a business share of renter’s insurance, utilities, and internet if applicable (not provided here).
  - Notes: Must be used regularly and exclusively for business, and serve as your principal place of business (including adm

in/management if you don’t have another fixed location). The home‑office deduction can’t create/expand a Schedule C loss; any excess can carry forward.
- Self‑employment tax and related deduction: Your photography profit is subject to SE tax (~15.3% of 92.35% of net profit). You also get an above‑the‑line deduction for half of that SE tax.
- Qualified Business Income (QBI) deduction: You likely qualify for up to 20% of your qualified business income (below the high‑income thresholds for 2024). Rough estimat

e with the actual home‑office method: a QBI deduction around $1,800–$2,200, depending on final profit and the half‑SE tax calculation.

Itemize or standard deduction?
- 2024 standard deduction (single): $14,600.
- Your likely itemized deductions are limited (no state income tax in TX, no mortgage interest given, charity $1,500). You’ll almost certainly be better off taking the standard deduction.

Rough numbers to give you a feel (not tax advice; final amounts depend on full details)
- If the $1,050 are bus

iness expenses and you use the actual home‑office method:
  - Schedule C profit ≈ $16,300 − $3,405 − $1,050 ≈ $11,845.
  - SE tax ≈ $1,675; half‑SE deduction ≈ $840.
  - Student loan interest deduction likely ≈ $1,900–$2,200 (phase‑out applies).
  - QBI deduction roughly ≈ $2,000–$2,200.
- If the $1,050 are W‑2 job expenses (not deductible) and you use the actual home‑office method:
  - Schedule C profit ≈ $12,895; SE tax ≈ $1,820; half‑SE ≈ $910.
  - Student loan interest deduction likely ≈ $1,900–$2,050.

- QBI deduction roughly ≈ $1,900–$2,100.

Forms you’ll need
- Form 1040.
- Schedule 1 (additional income/adjustments summary).
- Schedule C (Profit or Loss from Business) for photography income/expenses.
- Schedule SE (Self‑Employment Tax).
- Home office:
  - Form 8829 if you use the actual‑expense method.
  - No Form 8829 if you use the simplified method (you’ll enter the amount directly on Schedule C).
- Schedule B (Interest and Ordinary Dividends), because your bank interest exceeds $1,500.
- Form 8995

(QBI deduction), likely the simplified version given your income level.
- You’ll also use info returns you receive: W‑2 from Coastal Manufacturing, 1099‑INT (Capital One 360), 1099‑DIV and/or 1099‑INT (Merrill Edge), and any 1099‑NEC/1099‑K from clients/third‑party processors. Report all income even if you don’t receive a form. For student loan interest, you should receive Form 1098‑E (you can still claim it without the form if records support it).

Action items / quick clarifications
- Is the $1,050 in “u

nreimbursed expenses” for your photography business (e.g., supplies, mileage, software, phone/internet share)? If yes, those go on Schedule C.
- That $420 from Merrill Edge—was it interest, ordinary dividends, or qualified dividends? (If qualified dividends, part may be taxed at lower capital‑gains rates.)
- Do you pay renter’s insurance, utilities, or internet? If so, we can allocate the business share to increase your home‑office deduction under the actual method.
- Any other business costs (equipment, de

preciation, mileage, subscriptions, website, advertising)? Those would reduce your Schedule C profit and SE tax and may increase your student loan deduction.

If you’d like, I can:
- List out an exact expense checklist for your Schedule C and home office, or
- Draft an email to your tax preparer with these details and open questions.
